hook: Multi-agent is a scaling decision, not a vibe. Supervisors, handoffs, shared blackboards — **and the honest bill for what multi-agent costs you.**

scenes.title: One manager, many workers — **the default topology**
scenes.sub: The pattern behind most successful multi-agent systems
scenes.narration: The supervisor pattern: a central orchestrator agent receives the user's task, delegates to specialist workers — research, code, review — collects their outputs, and synthesizes the final result. If AG-10's orchestrator-workers sounded familiar, that's because this IS that pattern with agents as workers: dynamic decomposition, dispatched subtasks, judged completeness. Why it became the default: the control flow is legible — one decision-maker means one place to debug; workers are independently testable — each specialist evals against its own golden set; and skills scale horizontally — adding a new specialist doesn't retrain the system, it extends the roster. The supervisor's design determines the ceiling: its delegation quality, its context discipline — worker outputs compressed on return — and its termination criteria — when is the task ACTUALLY done, not just delegated?

layers.s: Decomposes · delegates · judges completeness · owns the user conversation
Research · coder · reviewer · each with own tools, prompts, evals
Workers return summaries + artifact pointers, not raw dumps (AG-13)

scenes.narration: Two failure modes to engineer against. Supervisor bottleneck: EVERYTHING flows through one context — the supervisor's window becomes the system's capacity limit; the same compaction and budget disciplines from AG-13 apply one level up, plus aggressive output compression from workers. Skill-boundary blur: specialists drift into each other's domains — the coder starts doing research, the reviewer starts rewriting — and quality quietly equalizes at mediocre; sharp system prompts per specialist, and a supervisor that ROUTES rather than lets workers self-select, keep the boundaries real. Framework note: LangGraph's supervisor nodes, CrewAI's crews and Microsoft Agent Framework's orchestration patterns all implement this topology directly — AG-15 compares them.

scenes.title: Handoffs: passing the conversation — **with its state**
scenes.sub: Transferring control between agents without losing the plot
scenes.narration: Not every delegation is subordinate. Sometimes control TRANSFERS: the triage agent realizes this is a billing issue and hands the conversation to the billing agent — which now owns the user thread. A handoff is more than forwarding messages: the receiving agent needs a proper briefing — the user's goal, what's been tried, key facts established, current state — written for a reader with zero shared context, because that's what the receiver has. OpenAI's Agents SDK elevated handoffs to a first-class primitive for exactly this: a typed transfer with an explicit payload, not an implicit chat-history dump. The design rules: brief, don't dump — a distilled handoff summary beats a hundred raw messages; receiver capabilities must cover the case — handoffs fail when the target agent lacks the tools the remaining task needs; and HAND BACK when wrong — a misrouted task should return gracefully, with the miss logged as routing-signal training data.

items.s: Distilled handoff: goal · tried · facts · state — written for a zero-context reader
Receiver must own the tools the remaining task needs — route by capability, not availability
Misroutes return with the miss logged — routing signal, not failure theater

scenes.narration: Handoffs versus tool-calls — the distinction that clarifies architecture: a tool-call is a WORKER doing a bounded task for the caller; a handoff is TRANSFER of ownership. Confuse them and you get the anti-pattern: an agent 'hands off' a subtask and then keeps managing it, doubling the coordination cost with none of the control. The routing table underneath deserves care: which agent owns which intents, how overlapping ownership is resolved — usually by making ONE agent the default owner per intent and documenting it. And measure handoff quality directly: golden conversations where the correct route is known; a system that misroutes thirty percent of billing questions has a routing bug, not a staffing problem. Handoffs are cheap to build and expensive to get wrong invisibly — instrument them.

scenes.title: Shared state & the blackboard: **agents that leave notes**
scenes.sub: A common workspace instead of message-passing everything
scenes.narration: Supervisors pass messages; blackboard architectures share a WORKSPACE: a common structured store — a document, a database, a scratchpad directory — that all agents read and write. Instead of agent A sending agent B a message, A writes a finding to the shared space; B reads what it needs when it needs it. The decoupling is the win: agents don't need to know each other exists — new specialists join by reading the same board; work proceeds asynchronously — no waiting on message round-trips; and the state is INSPECTABLE — a human can open the board and see exactly what the system knows, a debugging superpower message-passing lacks. The costs: concurrency discipline — two agents editing the same section need locks or merge semantics; staleness — readers must know when a section is final versus in-progress, so entries carry status and ownership metadata.

cards.s: Directed, synchronous, easy to trace · couples agents to each other's protocols · N² wiring as rosters grow
Decoupled, async, inspectable · needs concurrency + staleness discipline · the pattern behind agent coding tools' working files

scenes.narration: In practice, systems mix: supervisor uses messages for delegation and control; workers use the blackboard for the ARTIFACTS they're producing — AG-12's scratchpad, shared. This is exactly how agentic coding tools behave: the plan file, the notes, the task list — a blackboard the subagents read and write, while the orchestrator passes instructions directly. Design the board's schema deliberately: sections with owners and status fields — proposed, in-progress, verified — because the schema IS the coordination protocol; a board without status metadata becomes a pile of notes nobody trusts. And version it: when agents overwrite each other's work, diffable state turns he-said-she-said into a reviewable history — the same audit discipline as AG-09's append-only log.

scenes.title: When multi-agent hurts — **and the A2A escape hatch**
scenes.sub: The bill, itemized; interoperability as the hedge
scenes.narration: The honest bill for multi-agent. COST: each agent boundary is full LLM calls — a supervisor loop over four specialists can spend ten times a single-agent attempt on the same task. LATENCY: sequential delegation chains multiply response times — users wait through every hop. DEBUGGING: a failure in a multi-agent system is a distributed-systems failure — which agent, which message, which shared-state race? — the hardest class of bug to reproduce. And QUALITY: multi-agent doesn't automatically beat one well-prompted agent — for many tasks, a single agent with good tools and reflection outperforms a committee. The decision rule from AG-01, applied again: escalate to multi-agent ONLY when a single context demonstrably fails — different tool sets that can't share one window, genuinely parallel work, independent verification requirements. Otherwise, one agent, well-armed, wins.

items.s: Cost × agents · latency × hops · debugging becomes distributed-systems forensics · quality is NOT automatic
Multi-agent only on proven single-context failure: separate tool sets, true parallelism, independent verification
Agent-to-Agent interoperability — the MCP complement: MCP for tools, A2A for agents · 150+ adopting orgs

scenes.narration: On A2A — Agent2Agent, Google's donated protocol now stewarded with broad industry backing, crossing 150-plus adopting organizations: it standardizes how INDEPENDENT agents discover and talk to each other — agent cards describing capabilities, task-based messaging, status updates. The mental model pairing that stuck in 2026: MCP connects models to TOOLS; A2A connects agents to AGENTS. Your architecture benefits even without cross-company agents: building your specialists as A2A-speaking services keeps them portable across frameworks and vendors — the lock-in hedge AG-16 prices explicitly. Practical status: framework support is growing — Microsoft Agent Framework and CrewAI support it natively, Google ADK leads, LangGraph via adapters — verify current support before committing a design to it, but the direction is clear: agents, like tools before them, are becoming protocol-addressable.

scenes.title: Topologies in hand. Now the frameworks that implement them.
scenes.next: Reel 57 · Framework Landscape — LangGraph, MAF, CrewAI, Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK

recap: Supervisor is the default topology: one legible decision-maker, testable specialists, compressed returns — mind the supervisor's context bottleneck
Handoffs transfer ownership with distilled briefs and capability-checked routing; blackboards decouple agents via shared, status-annotated state
Multi-agent's bill is real: cost, latency, distributed debugging; A2A standardizes agent-to-agent interop as MCP did for tools

quiz.q: Why do worker returns to a supervisor need compression?
opts: The supervisor's context window is the system's capacity limit — raw worker dumps exhaust it after a few delegations
quiz.why: Everything flows through the supervisor's window: summaries plus artifact pointers are the only sustainable return format.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a handoff from a tool call between agents?
opts: A tool call is a bounded subtask for the caller; a handoff TRANSFERS ownership of the conversation — brief, capability-checked, and able to hand back
quiz.why: Ownership transfer changes everything: the receiver drives, the caller steps back — confusing the two doubles coordination cost.

quiz.q: What's the practical value of the A2A protocol for an internal system?
opts: Specialists built as A2A-speaking services stay portable across frameworks and vendors — a hedge against framework lock-in
quiz.why: Protocol-addressable agents outlive any single framework choice — the same portability argument that made MCP valuable for tools.

code.title: Supervisor loop with compressed returns and budgets
code.body:
async def supervisor(task: str):
    board = Blackboard(task_id=new_id())        # shared state (ch.3)
    budget = CostBudget(usd=2.00, wall=timedelta(minutes=10))

    while not budget.exhausted():
        plan = await llm(DELEGATE_PROMPT, task=task,
                         board=board.digest(),    # compressed view
                         roster=specialist_cards())
        if plan.done:
            return plan.answer

        results = await asyncio.gather(*[
            run_specialist(step, board) for step in plan.parallel_batch])
        for r in results:
            board.write(r.section,                 # pointer, not payload
                        summary=r.summary,
                        artifacts=r.artifact_paths,
                        status="verified" if r.self_checked else "proposed")
    return escalate(task, board.history())

# Specialists read/write sections; supervisor reads digests.
# The board — not message history — is the system's memory.
annot: board.digest() is the supervisor's context discipline: summaries + statuses, never raw payloads
Parallel batches per round: independent subtasks gather() together (PY-10), dependent ones wait
Budget enforced at the loop: cost AND wall-clock — long autonomy without a meter is a liability

notes:
# Architectures

## Supervisor
- Central orchestrator + specialists; legible control flow; independent evals.
- Bottleneck: supervisor context → compressed returns, digest reads.
- Keep specialist boundaries sharp: route, don't let workers self-select.

## Handoffs
- Transfer of ownership: distilled brief (goal/tried/facts/state).
- Capability-checked routing; graceful hand-backs with logged misses.

## Blackboard
- Shared workspace: decoupled, async, inspectable.
- Schema = coordination protocol: sections with owner + status.
- Mix: messages for control, board for artifacts.

## When multi-agent hurts
- Bill: cost × agents, latency × hops, distributed debugging, no auto-quality.
- Escalate only on proven single-context failure.
- **A2A**: agent-to-agent interop; MCP = tools, A2A = agents; portability hedge.
